extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning introductory set theory and relations
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, properties, and examples for indexed unions/intersections, relations, relation properties (reflexive/symmetric/transitive/etc.), equivalence relations/classes and partitions; aimed at building ability to state and prove basic facts about sets and relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed set intersection (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a collection {A_s : s ∈ 𝒮}, define the intersection over the index set 𝒮 by ⋂_{s∈𝒮} A_s = { x s.t. ∀ s ∈ 𝒮, x ∈ A_s }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the precise definition for intersection over an arbitrary index set (not necessarily countable); use the quantifier 'for all' to determine membership. Example: for real-indexed families A_x = [−x, x^2], apply the definition with s ∈ (0,10) or any chosen index set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed set union (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a collection {A_s : s ∈ 𝒮}, define the union over the index set 𝒮 by ⋃_{s∈𝒮} A_s = { x s.t. ∃ s ∈ 𝒮 with x ∈ A_s }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the existential quantifier to test membership: x is in the union if it belongs to at least one indexed set. Works for arbitrary index sets (including uncountable ones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection/union notation for sequences (tail notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When sets are indexed by the naturals with a starting index m (Am, Am+1, ...), one can write intersections/unions as Am ∩ Am+1 ∩ Am+2 ∩ ··· and Am ∪ Am+1 ∪ Am+2 ∪ ···.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recommends preferring precise indexed-notation (⋂_{k≥m} A_k, ⋃_{k≥m} A_k) over ellipses to keep things clear for the reader. Be careful: this notation presumes a countable index (naturals); it cannot be used to list uncountably many indices (e.g., real-indexed families).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: do not infer intersections from pointwise limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that the intersection of a family of shrinking intervals equals the limit-point interval suggested by endpoint limits; use the formal quantifier definitions to decide membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A_n = (−1/n, 1/n) has intersection containing 0, so is not empty, despite endpoints tending to 0. Avoid the dangerous naive reasoning that intersects to (0,0)=∅ by 'taking limits' — membership must satisfy 'x ∈ A_n for all n'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remark on uncountable indexing and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: When sets are indexed by uncountable sets (e.g., real numbers), one cannot write the union/intersection as an ordered list (Am, Am+1, ...); the reals are uncountable so such a list is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the general indexed notation ⋃_{s∈S} A_s and ⋂_{s∈S} A_s and be explicit about the index set; the text points readers to later material on uncountability for deeper justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empty relation and universal relation (special cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: On a set A, R = ∅ gives the empty relation (no ordered pairs satisfy it); R = A × A gives the universal relation (every ordered pair satisfies it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These extreme examples show the definition of relation as any subset of A×A; they are useful corner cases when reasoning about properties of relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a relation (on a single set)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on a set A is a subset R ⊆ A × A. If (x,y) ∈ R we write x ℛ y, otherwise x ℛ̸ y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes the idea of a relation as a set of ordered pairs; many familiar relations (equality, divisibility, order) fit into this framework. Use set-builder notation to define relations when helpful (e.g., R = { (x,x) | x ∈ R } for equality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a relation between different sets
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation between sets A and B is any subset R ⊆ A × B. If (x,y) ∈ R we denote x ℛ y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalisation covers relations like 'is a child of' (children vs parents) or membership a ∈ B (element vs set). Many constructions (functions) will use relations between different sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive property
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on A is reflexive when a ℛ a for every a ∈ A (quantified: ∀ a ∈ A, a ℛ a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualised as a loop at every node in dot-arrow diagrams. Use this quantifier form to check reflexivity; examples: '=' and '|' on integers are reflexive, '<' is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric property
rubrics_metrics.description: R is symmetric when for any a, b ∈ A, (a ℛ b) ⇒ (b ℛ a) (quantified: ∀ a,b ∈ A, a ℛ b =⇒ b ℛ a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualised as every arrow having a corresponding reverse arrow. Congruence and parity relations are symmetric; order relations like '<' are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive property
rubrics_metrics.description: R is transitive when for any a, b, c ∈ A, (a ℛ b) ∧ (b ℛ c) ⇒ (a ℛ c) (quantified: ∀ a,b,c ∈ A, ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualised as whenever there is a path x→y→z there must be x→z. Many important relations (equality, divisibility, ≤, congruence) are transitive. Note quantifiers do not require distinctness of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization guidance for relation properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dot-arrow diagrams to illustrate reflexive (loops on every node), symmetric (paired arrows), and transitive (if x→y and y→z then x→z) properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such diagrams are pedagogically helpful for small finite sets; they are illustrative and not intended to represent entire relations in large or infinite contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of properties for example relations (<, ≤, =, |)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the listed relations on appropriate sets the table indicates whether each is reflexive, symmetric, transitive: '<' is (false, false, true); '≤' is (true, false, true); '=' is (true, true, true); '|' (divides) is (true, false, true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete checks or counterexamples when assessing each property (e.g., '<' fails reflexivity since a < a is false).

rubrics_metrics.name: Total (connex) relation
rubrics_metrics.description: R is total/connex when ∀ a,b ∈ A, (a ℛ b) ∨ (b ℛ a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The relation '≤' on the reals is total. Use this to test whether every pair is comparable under the relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trichotomous relation
rubrics_metrics.description: R is trichotomous when ∀ a,b ∈ A, exactly one of (a ℛ b) or (b ℛ a) or (a = b) holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The relation '<' on the reals is trichotomous. Trichotomy gives a strong linear-order behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-symmetric relation
rubrics_metrics.description: R is anti-symmetric when ∀ a,b ∈ A, (a ℛ b) ∧ (b ℛ a) ⇒ a = b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ⊆ is anti-symmetric on sets; divisibility '|' is anti-symmetric on natural numbers but not on all integers (counterexample: a and −a). Check for required equality when both directions hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dense relation
rubrics_metrics.description: R is dense when ∀ a,b ∈ A with a ℛ b, there exists c ∈ A such that a ℛ c ∧ c ℛ b (the text writes: ∀a,b ∈ A, ∃ c ∈ A s.t. (a ℛ c) ∧ (c ℛ b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Density captures the idea of intermediate elements (e.g., rationals densely ordered). Use constructive existence arguments to prove density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruence modulo n is an equivalence relation (Theorem 9.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed n ∈ N, congruence modulo n is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (i.e., an equivalence relation): a ≡ b (mod n) iff n | (a − b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: reflexive because n | 0; symmetric because if n | (a−b) then n | (b−a); transitive by summing divisibility relations. Use divisibility algebra (write differences as multiples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on A is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence relations generalize equality; once established, they yield equivalence classes and partitions. Check all three properties when asserting equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence class [x] definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an equivalence relation R on A, the equivalence class of x is [x] = { y ∈ A : y ℛ x }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma: [x] is non-empty because x ∈ [x] (reflexivity). Theorem: [x] = [y] ⇔ x ℛ y (so any representative may be used). Equivalence classes are either equal or disjoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence classes partition the underlying set (partition theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of equivalence classes of an equivalence relation R on A forms a partition of A: each class non-empty, classes are pairwise disjoint, and their union is A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition of partition used: collection 𝒫 of non-empty subsets of A with union A and pairwise disjoint or equal. Use the class-equality/disjointness theorem and reflexivity to verify partition properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractions equality as an equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Define relation on fractions a/b and c/d by (a/b) ℛ (c/d) ⇔ ad = bc (equivalently they represent the same rational number). This relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses cross-multiplication and elementary algebra: reflexive (ab=ab), symmetric (ad=bc implies bc=ad), transitive (compose equalities and cancel nonzero denominators). This formalizes when distinct fraction representations denote the same rational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity relation (same parity) is an equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: On Z, define a relation by a ℛ b ⇔ a and b are both even or both odd (equivalently 2 | (a − b)). This relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses simple divisibility algebra: a−a=0 divisible by 2; if 2|(a−b) then 2|(b−a); if 2|(a−b) and 2|(b−c) then 2|(a−c). Use explicit k,ℓ integers to show transitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: equivalence classes for relation on R^2 (a+d = c+b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation on R^2 defined by (a,b) ℛ (c,d) ⇔ a + d = c + b is an equivalence relation; the equivalence class of (a,b) is the line y = x + (b−a) (all points with a+d = x+b rearrange to y = x + (b−a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: check reflexive/symmetric/transitive by algebraic manipulation; characterization of classes: (x,y) ∈ [(a,b)] iff y = x + (b − a), i.e., the classes are parallel lines of slope 1. Use substitution to exhibit class membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent equivalence classes using simple representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Since [x] = [y] whenever x ℛ y, choose the simplest representative of an equivalence class to present it (e.g., in congruence mod 5 use 0,1,2,3,4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is good exposition practice: be kind to the reader by presenting canonical/simpler representatives for classes rather than arbitrary ones.
